metadata.failure_mode: If the validation-loss-minimum iteration is not a reliable proxy for learning speed under the studied conditions, the precise quantitative speedup figures in conclusion 5 (e.g., "early-stopping occurs 38% earlier", "3.5× faster") would lose their quantitative foundation. The qualitative claim that winning tickets learn faster might still hold based on test accuracy curves, but the magnitude of the effect would be uncertain. The Occam's Hill analysis (performance improves with moderate pruning) would rely only on final accuracy comparisons, not on speed. The conclusion would be weakened in its quantitative claims, though the qualitative faster-learning observation (visible in Fig. 3, 5) would remain.
metadata.weakness_reason: The minimum-validation-loss criterion is a standard early-stopping heuristic, but its use as a proxy for learning speed has limitations: it conflates the speed of convergence of training loss with the speed of achieving low validation loss, and the validation loss minimum may occur before the network has reached high test accuracy if the model begins to overfit early. The paper acknowledges this in Appendix C but does not validate the metric against other speed measures (e.g., time to reach a specific accuracy threshold). The fact that deep net experiments do not use this metric suggests that the speed advantage may not be cleanly measurable under learning rate schedules. The paper's central quantitative speedup claims (e.g., "38% earlier early-stopping" for Lenet, "3.5× faster" for Conv-2) rely on this metric.

nodes.title: Early-stopping metric not applied to VGG-19 and Resnet-18; test accuracy at fixed iterations used instead, limiting speed comparison

nodes.content:
The comparison of iterative versus one-shot magnitude pruning with resetting on the Lenet-300-100 architecture for MNIST uses a fixed iterative pruning rate (20% of weights per layer per iteration) and compares it to a one-shot procedure that prunes directly to the same final sparsity levels. The iterative and one-shot procedures are not matched in total training budget: iterative involves multiple training rounds (each up to 50,000 iterations), while one-shot requires a single training run. The iterative pruning rate (20%) and the one-shot targets are not systematically varied to explore the full trade-off. Therefore, the conclusion that iterative pruning finds smaller and better winning tickets than one-shot pruning is based on a single comparative setting (iterative at 20% per iteration versus one-shot to the same final sparsities).
      Fig. 4c
      Fig. 9
      Fig. 10

metadata.failure_mode: If the advantage of iterative pruning is not general across different pruning rates and total training budgets, then conclusion 4 ("Iterative pruning finds smaller and better winning tickets than one-shot pruning") would be true only for the specific hyperparameter choices in the paper, rather than a general methodological insight. Practitioners might draw an overly strong conclusion that iterative is always necessary, when a well-chosen one-shot schedule might work comparably. The recommendation derived from this conclusion would be misleading.
metadata.weakness_reason: The paper's one-shot experiment uses the same pruning rate as iterative per layer. From Fig. 4c, one-shot prunes directly to the target sparsity and resets. The iterative vs one-shot comparison in Fig. 4c shows that iterative finds better accuracy and faster early-stopping across the sparsity range. However, the paper does not explore different numbers of iterative rounds (e.g., 20% pruning per round for 10 rounds gives a different trajectory than 10% per round for 20 rounds). The one-shot experiment might perform better if it used a different one-shot sparsity schedule (e.g., prune more aggressively early). The paper's claim about iterative superiority is empirically valid for the specific conditions but may not reflect a fundamental property of iterative pruning over one-shot; it could be an artifact of the specific pruning rates.

nodes.title: Iterative vs one-shot comparison on Lenet uses fixed 20% per-iteration rate and does not control for total training budget or vary rates

nodes.content:
The advantage of global magnitude pruning over layer-wise magnitude pruning (each at the same overall pruning rate of 20% per iteration) for discovering smaller winning tickets has been demonstrated only on the VGG-19 and Resnet-18 architectures for CIFAR10. These networks have highly uneven parameter distributions across layers (e.g., later layers of VGG-19 have orders of magnitude more parameters than early layers). The explanation that global pruning avoids bottlenecking small-parameter layers is specific to this setting; architectures with more uniform parameter distribution across layers or where global pruning might overly prune early feature extraction layers are not tested. The layer-wise comparison uses a uniform per-layer pruning rate (20% for all convolutional layers) instead of adjusting rates per layer size.
      Fig. 38
      Fig. 39

metadata.failure_mode: If global pruning does not outperform appropriately chosen layer-wise pruning on other architectures (e.g., architectures with no extreme parameter imbalance), then conclusion 8's claim that global pruning "finds smaller winning tickets in very deep, parameter-heterogeneous networks" is correct but potentially incomplete: it might be that the advantage is specifically for unbalanced architectures with uniform per-layer baselines, not a universal reason to prefer global pruning. The practical guidance would be restricted.
metadata.weakness_reason: The paper's appendix I.1 shows global vs layer-wise comparison for VGG-19 and Resnet-18. The pattern is clear for these two cases, but the rationale (small layers become bottlenecks) suggests that the advantage depends on the degree of parameter imbalance. Without testing on architectures with more balanced layers or with different imbalance patterns, the conclusion's scope is unknown. Additionally, the layer-wise baseline uses same pruning rate for all layers; a per-layer varying rate that accounts for parameter counts might approach global pruning's performance. The paper does not explore such adaptive layer-wise pruning.

nodes.title: Global vs layer-wise pruning advantage demonstrated only on VGG-19 and Resnet-18 with uneven parameter distributions; not tested on uniform architectures

nodes.content:
The definition of a winning ticket requires that the subnetwork $f(x;m\odot\theta_0)$ attains test accuracy $a' \ge a$ at iteration $j' \le j$, where $j$ is the early-stopping iteration (iteration of minimum validation loss) of the original network. For the VGG-19 and Resnet-18 experiments on CIFAR10, the early-stopping iteration is not reported for either the original network or the pruned subnetworks. Instead, test accuracy is presented at fixed training iterations (30K, 60K, 112K for VGG-19; 10K, 20K, 30K for Resnet-18). For example, VGG-19 with warmup finds subnetworks at $P_m=0.015$ that reach test accuracy near 91% at 112K iterations, while the original network trains for 160 epochs (112K iterations) without the early-stopping iteration being specified. Therefore, the condition $j' \le j$ is not verified for these deep networks; the results only demonstrate that winning tickets can match accuracy at the final training iteration, not that they do so in fewer iterations.
      Fig. 7
      Fig. 8

metadata.failure_mode: If one were to insist on the $j' \le j$ condition, the conclusion that winning tickets exist for VGG-19 and Resnet-18 would be unsupported in its full form. The paper's claim would need to be weakened to "winning tickets achieve comparable final accuracy at the end of the original network's training period" for deep networks. The faster-learning component would be supported only by early-iteration accuracy comparisons, not by a validated earlier occurrence of the minimum validation loss. This would narrow the conclusion's validity to small architectures (Lenet, Conv nets) for the full formal definition.
metadata.weakness_reason: The paper explicitly changes the evaluation methodology for deep networks: instead of the early-stopping metric used for Lenet and Conv nets, it plots test accuracy at predefined iteration milestones. This is a practical concession (deep nets exhibit overfitting patterns that make validation-loss-based early-stopping less straightforward due to learning rate schedules), but it means the claim that winning tickets train in "at most the same number of iterations" is not tested for these networks. The paper's visualization shows that winning tickets achieve higher accuracy at early milestones (e.g., 30K iterations for VGG-19 with warmup), which suggests faster learning, but this is not the same as showing that the minimal-validation-loss iteration occurs earlier. The formal claim in conclusion 1 thus rests on an incomplete verification for deep architectures.

nodes.title: Early-stopping iteration not reported for VGG-19 and Resnet-18; winning ticket condition j' ≤ j unverified

nodes.content:
The use of linear learning rate warmup (from 0 to the initial learning rate over $k$ iterations) to restore winning ticket discovery in deep networks has been demonstrated only for VGG-19 (with $k=10000$ and initial learning rate 0.1) and Resnet-18 (with $k=20000$ and initial learning rate 0.03) on CIFAR10. The warmup schedules were selected by manual exploration on the validation set and were not systematically optimized. It is unknown whether similar warmup schedules enable winning ticket discovery on other architectures, datasets, or learning rates, or whether alternative interventions (e.g., different optimizers, gradient clipping) could also suffice.
      Fig. 7
      Fig. 8
      Fig. 44
      Fig. 45

metadata.failure_mode: If warmup does not work for other deep architectures (e.g., Resnet-50 on ImageNet), then conclusion 6's statement that warmup is a practical mitigation would be limited in scope. The conclusion's claim about the sensitivity being overcome would be true only for the tested networks. The design insight (warmup helps) would not generalize.
metadata.weakness_reason: The paper's Appendix I.5 explores k values for both architectures and shows that larger k generally helps, but the set of architectures is only two. Given that the sensitivity to learning rate is itself a finding (deep nets require reduced learning rates), the warmup experiment is a single demonstration that this sensitivity can be overcome. Without broader validation, the conclusion that warmup "enables discovery at higher learning rates" may be specific to these two architectures and their specific training regimes. The paper acknowledges this as a future work direction.

nodes.title: Warmup mitigation tested only on VGG-19 and Resnet-18 with manually selected k; generalization unknown

nodes.content:
The claim that winning tickets learn faster than the original network (as defined by earlier early-stopping iteration) is supported for Lenet-300-100 on MNIST and Conv-2/4/6 on CIFAR10, where the iteration of minimum validation loss is measured. For VGG-19 and Resnet-18 on CIFAR10, the early-stopping iteration is not computed or reported; instead, test accuracy is evaluated at fixed training checkpoints (e.g., 30K, 60K, 112K for VGG-19). At these checkpoints, winning tickets (with warmup) sometimes achieve higher test accuracy than the unpruned network (e.g., VGG-19 at 30K iterations), which is suggestive of faster learning but does not directly verify that the winning ticket reaches its own minimum validation loss earlier. Thus, the learning speed advantage for deep networks is qualitative and relies on a different metric.
      Fig. 7
      Fig. 8

metadata.failure_mode: If the faster-learning claim for deep networks is challenged, the evidence is limited to early-iteration accuracy comparisons, which may not fully capture the notion of learning speed (e.g., a network may plateau at lower accuracy initially but converge faster later). Conclusion 5's scope would be effectively limited to the Lenet and Conv networks for the quantitative learning-speed advantage; for deep networks, only the qualitative suggestion of faster early learning remains. The Occam's Hill pattern for deep nets would only be about final accuracy, not speed.
metadata.weakness_reason: The paper switches from reporting early-stopping iteration (for Lenet, Conv) to reporting accuracy at fixed iterations (for VGG-19, Resnet-18), which is a different kind of metric. While the paper mentions that the early-stopping measure is entangled with learning rate schedules for deep nets (Appendix I), it does not provide an alternative quantitative measure of speed for these experiments. The claim that deep net winning tickets learn faster is supported by instances where winning tickets have higher accuracy at early milestones, but this is not a direct measure of convergence speed. Without a consistent metric or alternative quantification, the faster-learning claim for deep networks is less precise than for smaller networks.

nodes.title: Faster learning claim for VGG-19 and Resnet-18 not verified with early-stopping metric; based on accuracy at fixed checkpoints

nodes.content:
The empirical structural and initialization properties of winning tickets described in the conclusion (bimodal weight distributions, larger weight changes from initialization to final state, proportional incoming connectivity, uneven outgoing connectivity, and noise robustness) have been characterized only on the fully-connected Lenet-300-100 architecture for MNIST, under Adam (learning rate 0.0012) and SGD (learning rate 0.8) optimization. The convolutional architectures (Conv-2, Conv-4, Conv-6, VGG-19, Resnet-18) used in other experiments were not analyzed for these properties. Therefore, these properties have not been shown to be general across feed-forward architectures; they may be specific to the fully-connected structure of Lenet on the MNIST dataset.
      Fig. 15
      Fig. 16
      Fig. 19
      Fig. 20
      Fig. 21
      Fig. 23
      Fig. 25

metadata.failure_mode: If the properties turn out to be specific to fully-connected layers (e.g., bimodality arises from the nature of fully-connected weights rather than a general lottery ticket property), then conclusion 7 would be misleadingly broad. The properties would still be accurate descriptions of Lenet winning tickets, but they would not constitute a general characterization of winning tickets in feed-forward networks. The paper's claim ("These structural phenomena are consistent across optimizers (Adam, SGD) and the Lenet/Conv experiments analyzed") is partly true: the "Conv experiments" are Lenet-like (fully-connected) not convolutional networks.
metadata.weakness_reason: The paper's Appendix F is titled "Examining Winning Tickets" and all figures there (15-25) use the Lenet architecture. The paper states "Throughout this Appendix, we study the winning tickets from the Lenet architecture trained on MNIST." The choice is practical (tractability of analysis), but it means that the detailed characterizations of weight distributions, connectivity, noise robustness, etc., are not demonstrated for convolutional layers. Convolutional layers have a different connectivity structure (shared weights through filters, spatial locality), so it is plausible that the bimodal distribution of surviving weights might differ. The paper does not provide evidence that these properties hold for the winning tickets found in the convolutional experiments that support conclusions 1-6.

nodes.title: Structural properties of winning tickets characterized only on Lenet-300-100 for MNIST; not on convolutional architectures

nodes.content: On the Lenet, Conv-2, Conv-4, and Conv-6 architectures, holding the sparse mask $m$ fixed but resampling the parameters from the original initialization distribution $\\mathcal{D}_\\theta$ (three reinitializations per trial, five trials per architecture) results in substantially worse training dynamics: for Lenet at $P_m=21.1\\%$, the winning ticket reaches minimum validation loss 2.51× faster and achieves ~0.5 percentage points higher test accuracy than the reinitialized mask; for the Conv architectures, reinitialized masks degrade in accuracy and learn more slowly as pruning increases. This comparison directly controls for the connectivity structure (the mask) and isolates the effect of the original initialization values. The experiment is repeated across multiple architectures and optimizers, strengthening the generalizability of the conclusion that initialization is a crucial component of the winning ticket phenomenon.

metadata.credit: This experiment preempts the alternative explanation that the winning ticket effect is due solely to the sparse connectivity pattern (the mask). Without this control, one could argue that any sparse subnetwork of the right architecture would train well from scratch; the reinitialization experiment shows that the same mask with different initialization values fails. The layer of credibility underwritten is the mechanistic/attribution layer—it establishes that initialization is causally important (under the studied conditions). The scope is strong: the pattern holds across all tested architectures (fully-connected and convolutional), and the quantitative gap between winning ticket and reinitialized performance widens with increased sparsity (pruning), which is consistent with growing importance of initialization as the network becomes smaller. This control is directly load-bearing for conclusion 3; without it, the conclusion would lack causal evidence.

nodes.title: Random reinitialization control demonstrates initialization importance

nodes.content: On Conv-2, Conv-4, and Conv-6 architectures trained with dropout rate 0.5 (Adam with learning rates 0.0003, 0.0002, 0.0002 respectively), the iterative pruning with resetting procedure continues to find winning tickets that improve upon the dropout-trained unpruned network's test accuracy (by up to 2.3, 4.6, and 4.7 percentage points respectively) and in most cases also exhibit faster learning (early-stopping intervals decrease, though less dramatically for Conv-2). This demonstrates that the winning ticket phenomenon is not limited to standard (non-regularized) training; it occurs even when the training process is explicitly randomizing subnetwork choices at each iteration via dropout, which is a challenging setting for the hypothesis that specific subnetworks are critical.

metadata.credit: This experiment preempts the concern that winning tickets are an artifact of overparameterized, overfitting networks (since dropout reduces overfitting). The fact that winning tickets further improve accuracy on top of dropout's gains suggests that the two mechanisms are complementary. The layer of credibility is generalization—the conclusion that winning tickets exist is shown to hold under a qualitatively different training setup (strong regularization). Without this experiment, the scope of conclusion 1 would be limited to standard training; with it, the scope includes regularized training, increasing confidence that the phenomenon is more general.

nodes.title: Dropout experiments show winning tickets exist under strong regularization

nodes.content: For the Lenet architecture on MNIST, the paper compares three conditions: (a) winning tickets from iterative pruning with original initialization, (b) the same masks randomly reinitialized, and (c) random sparse subnetworks of equal size (randomly sampled weights, trained from scratch). The random sparse subnetworks (condition c) perform worse than winning tickets (condition a) and comparably to or worse than randomly reinitialized masks (condition b) across the sparsity range. For the Conv-2, Conv-4, and Conv-6 networks, the random sparse subnetworks also perform comparably to random reinitialization, and winning tickets outperform both. This control establishes that the iterative pruning procedure does more than simply produce a sparse architecture of a given size; it identifies a specific subnetwork that is particularly trainable, beyond what random subnetwork sampling achieves.

metadata.credit: This control preempts the hypothesis that any sparse subnetwork of the same size would train as well (the "architecture-only" hypothesis). It shows that the mask itself matters, not just the sparsity level. Without this control, one could argue that the winning ticket effect is simply a size-dependent phenomenon (smaller networks train well at the sizes found). The layer of credibility is attribution—the winning ticket's advantage is attributed to the specific mask+initialization combination, not just to reduced size. The experiment supports conclusion 1 by showing that the discovered subnetworks perform better than random sparse networks of equal size, strengthening the claim that the procedure uncovers something special.

nodes.title: Random sparsity baseline shows iterative pruning finds special subnetworks

nodes.content: The iterative pruning with resetting experiment is repeated on the Lenet architecture with Adam, SGD, and SGD with momentum across a range of learning rates (e.g., Adam from 2.5e-05 to 6.4e-03, SGD from 0.05 to 1.6). In all cases, the lottery ticket pattern (learning becomes faster and accuracy increases with moderate pruning) is present, though the optimal learning rates vary. The paper also explores different pruning rates (10% to 80%), initialization distributions (Glorot vs fixed-variance Gaussians), and network sizes (varying hidden layer widths). Across these variations, winning tickets are consistently found, although their specific sizes and performance advantages vary. This extensive robustness check supports the claim that the existence of winning tickets is not an artifact of a specific hyperparameter choice.

metadata.credit: This collection of experiments preempts the concern that the winning ticket phenomenon is specific to the particular hyperparameters chosen in the main experiments (Adam, 1.2e-3, Glorot initialization, 300/100 units). The demonstration across many hyperparameters strengthens the claim that the phenomenon is a general property of the studied architectures. Without these robustness checks, the conclusion would be more fragile. The layer of credibility is the qualitative existence claim—the fact that winning tickets appear under such diverse settings makes it unlikely that they are a fluke of a particular configuration. The scope is bounded to the architectures tested, but within that scope the robustness is substantial.

nodes.title: Winning ticket phenomenon holds across diverse optimizers and learning rates

nodes.content: On the Lenet architecture, Gaussian noise with varying standard deviations (0.5σ, σ, 2σ, 3σ, where σ is the layer's initialization standard deviation) is added to the winning ticket's initialization values before training. The winning ticket's test accuracy remains largely unchanged under 0.5σ noise, degrades gradually under larger noise, and remains above the performance of randomly reinitialized masks even under 3σ noise. This graded degradation shows that the original initialization values provide a specific advantage that diminishes smoothly as they are perturbed, ruling out the possibility that the winning ticket effect relies on an extremely precise set of values that are trivially disrupted. The experiment is repeated with 5 winning tickets per condition.

metadata.credit: This experiment preempts the extreme alternative that the winning ticket's advantage comes from an extremely specific and brittle set of initialization values. By showing gradual degradation, it supports the conclusion that initialization matters but is not hyper-specific; the advantage is associated with the distribution of values (e.g., being bimodal with a certain sign asymmetry) rather than each individual exact number. Without this experiment, one might think that any small deviation would destroy the effect, which would make the conclusion less scientifically interesting. The layer of credibility is the mechanistic explanation of the initial values: the paper argues the initial values are "special" in a robust sense, and this perturbation supports that. The scope is Lenet only, but it strengthens the conclusion's causal claim about initialization.

nodes.title: Graded sensitivity to initialization perturbation supports importance of original values

nodes.content: On VGG-19 and Resnet-18 for CIFAR-10, under the training hyperparameters from Section 4 (SGD with momentum, learning rates 0.01 and 0.1 with warmup), global magnitude pruning of all convolutional weights together is compared against layer-wise pruning at the same per-iteration rate (20%). For VGG-19, global pruning finds winning tickets down to P_m ≈ 1.5% whereas layer-wise pruning only reaches P_m ≈ 6.9%. For Resnet-18, global pruning finds winning tickets at P_m ≈ 11.8% while layer-wise pruning gives smaller sparsity advantages. These quantitative comparisons are shown for multiple training iterations (30K, 60K, 112K for VGG-19; 10K, 20K, 30K for Resnet-18) and across three learning-rate conditions (0.1, 0.01, 0.1 with warmup).

metadata.credit: This experiment directly supports conclusion 8 by providing a controlled comparison that isolates the pruning strategy (global vs layer-wise) while keeping all other hyperparameters fixed. The failure mode it preempts is that the global pruning advantage might be an artifact of different architectures or training conditions; showing the same pattern on two different deep architectures (VGG-19 and Resnet-18) under multiple learning rates strengthens the claim. Without this controlled comparison, the advantage of global pruning would be speculative. The layer of credibility is the quantitative claim about sparsity fractions—the specific numbers (1.5% vs 6.9% for VGG-19) are load-bearing for conclusion 8. The scope of credit is limited to the studied architectures, but the controlled design makes the conclusion credible within that scope.

nodes.title: Global pruning controlled comparison on two deep architectures

nodes.content: On the Lenet architecture for MNIST, the paper directly compares iterative pruning (20% per iteration, with resetting) and one-shot pruning (directly pruning to target sparsity and resetting) at the same final sparsity levels. The iterative winning tickets consistently reach lower early-stopping iterations and higher test accuracy than one-shot winning tickets across the sparsity range from 100% down to about 1% of weights remaining. The one-shot experiment is run with the same hyperparameters (Adam, learning rate 0.0012, same pruning rate per layer as iterative). The comparison is also repeated on the Conv-2, Conv-4, and Conv-6 networks (Appendix B), confirming the pattern.

metadata.credit: This experiment supports conclusion 4 by providing a clean comparison where the only difference is the number of pruning rounds (iterative vs one-shot). Without this comparison, one could argue that the iterative advantage is simply due to training the network for more total time (since iterative uses many training runs). The paper controls for this implicitly: one-shot uses one training run to reach the same final mask size, while iterative uses many runs. The fact that iterative still outperforms shows that the iterative process of repeatedly training, pruning, and resetting yields different masks than a one-shot prune at the same target sparsity. The layer of credibility is the existence of a difference: iterative finds smaller winning tickets. The scope is limited to Lenet and Conv nets with the specific pruning rates; the quantitative numbers (e.g., smallest winning ticket size) are tied to those settings.

nodes.title: Controlled comparison of iterative and one-shot pruning

nodes.content: On VGG-19 for CIFAR-10 under standard training (SGD with momentum, initial learning rate 0.1, no warmup), iterative pruning fails to find winning tickets. Applying linear learning rate warmup from 0 to 0.1 over 10,000 iterations restores winning ticket discovery: at P_m ≥ 1.5%, the winning tickets match or exceed the accuracy of the original unpruned network. On Resnet-18, warmup of 20,000 iterations at learning rate 0.03 (up from 0.01 without warmup) enables winning tickets at P_m ≥ 11.8% approaching 90.5% test accuracy. The experiment varies the number of warmup iterations (k = 0, 1000, 2000, 5000, 10000, 20000 for VGG-19; k = 0, 5000, 20000 for Resnet-18) and shows that warmup is necessary and sufficient for the phenomenon at higher learning rates.

metadata.credit: This experiment, reported in Section 4 and Appendix I.5, directly supports conclusion 6 by showing that the sensitivity to learning rate can be overcome by a specific intervention (warmup), which itself is a subject of study. The controlled comparison (same learning rate, same architecture, with and without warmup) establishes that the failure at high learning rates is not intrinsic to the architecture but to the training dynamics. Without this demonstration, conclusion 6 would only state the limitation (sensitivity) without a constructive result; the warmup provides both evidence for the limitation's nature and a potential path forward. The layer of credibility is both the existence of the sensitivity and the existence of a mitigation. The scope of credit is limited to the tested architectures and learning rates, but the controlled design gives confidence that warmup is a genuine remedy.

nodes.title: Learning rate warmup restores winning ticket discovery for deep networks

steps.reasoning: Define the network, initialization distribution, and mask notation used throughout the derivation: let $f(x;\\theta)$ denote a feed-forward neural network with parameters $\\theta$, and let the random initialization be $\\theta_0 \\sim \\mathcal{D}_\\theta$ where $\\mathcal{D}_\\theta$ is the initialization distribution (Gaussian Glorot initialization is used in the experiments). Define a binary mask $m\\in\\{0,1\\}^{|\\theta|}$ and the elementwise product $m\\odot\\theta$ to represent pruning (surviving parameters keep their values; pruned parameters are zeroed). Define the sparsity fraction $P_m = \\frac{\\|m\\|_0}{|\\theta|}$ as the fraction of original parameters that remain after pruning.

State the target empirical desiderata that identify a "winning ticket": when training the dense network $f(x;\\theta)$ initialized at $\\theta_0$ with stochastic gradient descent (SGD) (or other optimizers used), it reaches minimum validation loss at iteration $j$ with test accuracy $a$; a subnetwork $f(x;m\\odot\\theta_0)$ is a winning ticket if, when trained in isolation with $m$ fixed and initialization $m\\odot\\theta_0$, it reaches minimum validation loss at iteration $j'$ with test accuracy $a'$ satisfying $j'\\le j$ and $a'\\ge a$, while having $\\|m\\|_0 \\ll |\\theta|$.

Describe the pruning-and-resetting identification procedure (iterative magnitude-based pruning with resetting) used to find candidate masks $m$: initialize $\\theta = \\theta_0$, train the network to obtain $\\theta_j$, prune a fraction $p\\%$ of the parameters by magnitude (removing the lowest-magnitude weights to create a mask), and then reset the surviving weights to their original initial values in $\\theta_0$, forming $m\\odot\\theta_0$. For iterative pruning, repeat cycles of training, pruning a smaller fraction each round (so that after $n$ rounds total fraction $p\\%$ has been removed), and resetting to $\\theta_0$ after each pruning round. This variant—iterative magnitude pruning with resetting—is the principal procedure evaluated in the paper.  Han et al. (2015)

Record the experimental claim that the procedure in the previous step produces subnetworks that meet the winning-ticket desiderata on the studied image-classification tasks (MNIST and CIFAR10): the authors report repeatedly that iterative magnitude-based pruning followed by resetting the surviving weights to their original random initial values uncovers sparse subnetworks $f(x;m\\odot\\theta_0)$ that, when trained from those original initializations, reach validation-based early-stopping no later than and test accuracy no worse than the corresponding unpruned network trained from $\\theta_0$ under the optimizers and regimes examined in the paper. This claim is the central empirical statement of the paper and is supported throughout Sections 2–4 and the appendices by experiments on Lenet (MNIST), Conv-2/4/6 (CIFAR10), VGG-19 (CIFAR10), and Resnet-18 (CIFAR10). Fig. 1

Summarize experimental evidence on fully-connected and convolutional architectures showing the key properties $j'\\le j$ and $a'\\ge a$: for the fully-connected Lenet on MNIST, iterative pruning yields masks with $P_m$ where the pruned-and-reset networks reach the iteration of minimum validation loss (the paper's early-stopping proxy) earlier than or equal to the unpruned network and reach equal or higher test accuracy at that iteration; analogous behavior is observed for Conv-2/Conv-4/Conv-6 on CIFAR10 where iteratively-pruned-and-reset subnetworks learn faster and in many cases achieve higher test accuracy than the original dense networks. These comparisons use the iteration of minimum validation loss as $j$ and the test accuracy at that iteration as $a$, as explicitly defined by the authors. Fig. 3

Provide quantitative illustrative examples from the experiments that instantiate the general claim: the Lenet experiments show winning tickets at various $P_m$ values (e.g., $P_m = 51.3\\%$ and $P_m = 21.1\\%$) that reach early-stopping sooner and reach higher test accuracy than the unpruned network; Conv-2/Conv-4/Conv-6 experiments show winning tickets that reach minimum validation loss up to $3.5\\times$ faster and achieve test accuracy improvements (see subsequent figures and text for the particular $P_m$ values). These concrete experimental outcomes substantiate the general statement that the iterative pruning+reset procedure uncovers trainable subnetworks satisfying $j'\\le j$ and $a'\\ge a$ in the studied settings. Fig. 5

Note the procedural contrast that validates the importance of resetting to original initialization: the authors compare (a) training the pruned mask after resetting surviving weights to $\\theta_0$ and (b) training the pruned mask when the surviving weights retain their trained values or are randomly reinitialized; empirical results show that resetting to the original initialization (the procedure above) is the variant that yields subnetworks with the winning-ticket properties most consistently across the examined tasks and hyperparameters, reinforcing that the claimed discovery method is iterative magnitude pruning with resetting. Fig. 4

Conclude from the combination of the formal definition, the iterative magnitude pruning+reset procedure, and the presented experimental evidence across architectures and optimization regimes that iterative magnitude-based pruning with resetting uncovers subnetworks (called winning tickets) that, when trained in isolation from their original random initializations, match or exceed the original dense networks' early-stopping iteration and test accuracy for the image-classification tasks studied (MNIST and CIFAR10) under the optimizers and regimes in the paper.

Begin from the established empirical statement that iterative magnitude pruning with resetting uncovers winning-ticket subnetworks (the result of Conclusion 1 is treated as known and available for use). Recall the notation $P_m = \\frac{\\|m\\|_0}{|\\theta|}$ as the fraction of original parameters remaining in mask $m$.

Report the aggregate empirical size ranges observed across the examined architectures: the authors state that, across the fully-connected Lenet and the convolutional Conv-2/Conv-4/Conv-6 architectures, winning tickets are commonly found at parameter fractions on the order of roughly 10–20% ($P_m \\approx 0.1\\text{–}0.2$), and that some winning tickets remain effective down to a few percent of parameters in certain experiments. This summary appears in the Abstract and is supported by the detailed experimental plots in Sections 2 and 3. Fig. 1

Provide specific experimental instances cited by the authors that instantiate the stated ranges: in the Lenet experiments the authors report winning tickets with $P_m$ values such as $51.3\\%$, $21.1\\%$, $13.5\\%$, and a regression back to original performance at $P_m=3.6\\%$; Conv-2 and Conv-4 experiments show regimes where test accuracy remains above the original when $P_m > 2\\%$ and report best-learning-speed and best-accuracy improvements at $P_m$ values below 10% (for example, Conv-2 best early-stopping at $P_m=8.8\\%$ and best test-accuracy improvement at $P_m=4.6\\%$). These numbers are presented in Sections 2 and 3 and in the associated figures. Fig. 3

Note examples where winning tickets are found at still smaller fractions for deeper networks when additional hyperparameter modifications are applied: for VGG-19 with global pruning and linear learning-rate warmup, the authors report subnetworks at $P_m \\ge 1.5\\%$ that match or nearly match original accuracy under the selected regimes; this is reported in Section 4 and shown in the VGG-19 plots. For Resnet-18 with warmup and tuned learning rate, winning tickets are found at larger but still reduced $P_m$ values (examples discussed in Section 4). Fig. 7

Clarify the conditional nature of these empirical ranges: the authors emphasize that the observed $P_m$ thresholds depend on architecture, optimizer, pruning strategy (layer-wise vs global), and optimization hyperparameters (learning rates, warmup). Thus the 10–20% characterization is a typical empirical regime across the architectures and hyperparameters the authors studied, with deeper networks sometimes admitting winning tickets at still smaller fractions under additional adjustments (global pruning, warmup). Fig. 38

Conclude that, based on the iterative pruning+reset experiments across Lenet and Conv-2/4/6 and the deeper VGG-19/Resnet-18 investigations, the winning tickets discovered empirically are substantially smaller than the original networks, commonly in the 10–20% range and occasionally down to single-digit percentages or lower (e.g., VGG-19 at $P_m\\ge 1.5\\%$ under global pruning and warmup) for the regimes tested.

Treat the existence of winning tickets from iterative pruning+reset as established (Conclusion 1 is known). Define the random reinitialization experiment: given a discovered mask $m$, sample a new initialization $\\theta_0' \\sim \\mathcal{D}_\\theta$ (the same initialization distribution used originally), and train the pruned network $f(x;m\\odot\\theta_0')$ in isolation to compare its learning dynamics and test accuracy to $f(x;m\\odot\\theta_0)$.

Report the principal empirical observation about reinitialization: across multiple architectures and experiments, when the authors hold the mask $m$ fixed but resample parameters from the original initialization distribution (i.e., reinitialize surviving weights randomly), the resulting networks train more slowly and achieve lower test accuracy than the corresponding winning ticket trained from its original $\\theta_0$. This observation is directly reported in Sections 2 and 3 and illustrated in the dashed curves (reinitializations) versus solid curves (winning tickets) in the figures. Fig. 3

Give the quantitative example provided for Lenet that the authors use to quantify the effect: at $P_m = 21.1\\%$ on Lenet, the winning ticket (trained from the original initialization $\\theta_0$) reaches minimum validation loss 2.51\\times faster than the same mask with random reinitialization $\\theta_0'$, and the winning ticket is approximately 0.5 percentage points more accurate in test accuracy at early-stopping. These numerical comparisons are explicitly stated in Section 2 when discussing the random reinitialization experiments. Fig. 4

Summarize analogous observations for convolutional networks: in Conv-2/Conv-4/Conv-6 experiments, randomly reinitializing surviving weights causes the pruned networks to learn more slowly and to lose test accuracy as pruning increases; in some convolutional cases the reinitialized masks' test accuracy drops off from the original accuracy at higher $P_m$ (i.e., they fail sooner) than the winning tickets trained from their original initializations. These comparative trends are shown in the Conv-2/4/6 plots. Fig. 5

Draw the interpretive conclusion furnished by the authors: because preserving only the sparse structure (the mask $m$) while randomizing initial values degrades learning dynamics and test accuracy substantially, the success of a winning ticket is not explained solely by its connectivity pattern; the original initial parameter values (the particular random numbers assigned by $\\theta_0$ to the surviving connections) are crucial to the winning ticket effect in the experiments reported.

Treat the identification procedure of iterative pruning with resetting and the existence of winning tickets as established (Conclusion 1). Define one-shot pruning as the alternative procedure described by the authors: train the dense network once, prune $p\\%$ of the smallest-magnitude weights, and reset the surviving weights to their original initial values (i.e., perform pruning in a single shot rather than iteratively pruning smaller fractions across multiple rounds).

Describe the authors' experimental comparison between iterative pruning and one-shot pruning: in Section 2 the authors run both one-shot and iterative pruning experiments on Lenet and compare early-stopping iteration and test accuracy of the resulting pruned-and-reset networks across a range of $P_m$ values. The results are plotted and contrasted (one-shot in green, iterative in blue in the figures cited). Fig. 4

State the empirical outcome of this comparison: one-shot pruning can find trainable sparse subnetworks over a limited range of $P_m$ (i.e., it sometimes produces networks that learn effectively when reset), but iterative pruning consistently locates subnetworks that are sparser (smaller $P_m$) and that either match or exceed the original network's accuracy and learning speed at those smaller sizes. The figures show that the iterative-pruning curves extend to lower $P_m$ with better early-stopping and test-accuracy performance than the one-shot curves.

Provide concrete evidence phrases used by the authors to support the claim: the authors state that "iterative pruning finds winning tickets that match the accuracy of the original network at smaller sizes than does one-shot pruning" and show that one-shot pruning finds winning tickets only over a narrower range of $P_m$, whereas iterative pruning yields smaller, higher-performing winning tickets for the same architectures and hyperparameters. The plotted comparisons and the authors' textual summary constitute the basis for the claim. Fig. 4

Conclude that iterative magnitude pruning with resetting is empirically superior to one-shot magnitude pruning+reset for discovering smaller and higher-performing winning tickets under the experimental regimes evaluated: iterative pruning locates sparser masks $m$ (smaller $P_m$) that better match or exceed the original network's accuracy and learning speed than one-shot pruning.

Start from the upstream results: Conclusions 1 (existence of winning tickets via iterative pruning+reset) and 2 (typical winning-ticket sizes) are taken as established premises for this derivation. Recall the early-stopping proxy definition: the iteration of minimum validation loss is used as the measure of learning speed ($j$), and test accuracy at that iteration is used to measure generalization ($a$).

Report the central empirical pattern the authors name "Occam's Hill": as the fraction of parameters remaining $P_m$ decreases from 100% down into moderate sparsity, the pruned-and-reset networks initially learn faster (reach the early-stopping iteration sooner) and often achieve higher test accuracy, producing a hill-shaped relationship where performance first improves and then, under extreme pruning, deteriorates. The authors explicitly label this empirical curve "Occam's Hill" and provide plots showing early-stopping iteration and test accuracy as functions of $P_m$. Fig. 3

Give numeric Lenet evidence for faster learning: in the Lenet iterative-pruning experiment the authors report that early-stopping occurs 38% earlier at $P_m = 21\\%$ than for the unpruned original network; they also report that further pruning beyond an optimal range slows learning and that at $P_m = 3.6\\%$ performance returns to or below the original network's level. These specific quantities are reported in Section 2 and in the Lenet figures. Fig. 4a

Provide numeric Conv-net evidence for faster learning and improved test accuracy: Conv-2 achieved minimum validation loss at best 3.5× faster when $P_m = 8.8\\%$, Conv-4 at 3.5× faster at $P_m = 9.2\\%$, and Conv-6 at 2.5× faster at $P_m = 15.1\\%$. Test accuracy improvements in these Conv experiments peaked at up to 3.4 percentage points (Conv-2 at $P_m = 4.6\\%$), 3.5 percentage points (Conv-4 at $P_m = 11.1\\%$), and 3.3 percentage points (Conv-6 at $P_m = 26.4\\%$). These values are reported explicitly in Section 3 and the associated figures. Fig. 5

Explain how generalization is measured and why the authors claim improved generalization: the authors compare training accuracy and test accuracy at early-stopping and at the final training iteration; they note that training accuracy typically reaches near 100% for many pruned networks (except extremely pruned cases), but that winning tickets still exhibit higher test accuracy and a reduced gap between training and test accuracy, indicating better generalization. This observation is supported by training-accuracy plots in the appendices showing that training accuracy reaches 100% for $P_m \\ge 2\\%$ while test accuracy remains higher for winning tickets, thus decreasing the generalization gap. Fig. 4bFig. 13

Synthesize the observations into the Occam's Hill description: the authors interpret the empirical pattern as an "Occam's Hill" where moderate pruning removes excess capacity that may contribute to overfitting while preserving or highlighting well-initialized subnetworks that learn efficiently; but extreme pruning removes too much capacity and degrades both learning speed and accuracy. They connect this empirical shape to classical ideas that compression can improve generalization and cite related theoretical work.

Conclude that, empirically in the experiments presented, winning tickets often learn faster (reach the early-stopping iteration sooner) and generalize at least as well as, and sometimes better than, the original dense networks, producing an Occam's Hill phenomenon in which performance improves up to an optimal sparsity and then falls off under extreme pruning.

Treat the baseline result that iterative pruning+reset can find winning tickets (Conclusion 1) as known. Define the hyperparameter sensitivity phenomenon to investigate: the dependence of winning-ticket discovery on optimization hyperparameters, especially the initial learning rate and the use of learning-rate warmup.

Report the empirical observation on deep architectures (VGG-19 and Resnet-18): when trained with the commonly used high initial learning rate (for these architectures the standard is $0.1$), iterative pruning with reset failed to find winning tickets (i.e., pruned-and-reset networks did not match the unpruned network's performance), whereas lowering the initial learning rate to $0.01$ restored the winning-ticket behavior in iterative pruning experiments. This observation is explicitly described in Section 4 and shown in the VGG-19 and Resnet-18 plots. Fig. 7Fig. 8

Describe the remediation via learning-rate warmup that the authors apply: they use linear warmup of the learning rate from 0 up to the target initial learning rate over $k$ iterations (i.e., linearly increase the step size during the first $k$ training iterations). The authors test warmup schedules with various $k$ values and report that warmup allows iterative pruning to find winning tickets at higher nominal initial learning rates that otherwise fail.

Give the concrete warmup-enabled empirical examples cited: for VGG-19 trained at initial learning rate $0.1$, adding linear warmup over $k=10000$ iterations enables iterative pruning to find subnetworks that match or approach the original accuracy at $P_m\\ge 1.5\\%$ (the authors report that warmup improves unpruned-network accuracy by about one percentage point and makes winning tickets possible at $P_m\\ge 1.5\\%$). Similarly, for Resnet-18 the authors report that warmup with $k=20000$ and an initial learning rate of $0.03$ leads to winning tickets at larger $P_m$ values (e.g., $P_m\\approx 27\\%$ matching original accuracy under those hyperparameters). These numerics and configurations are provided in Section 4 and in Appendix I where warmup experiments are explored. Fig. 7Fig. 8

Note the related methodological change for deep networks: the authors also change from layer-wise pruning to global pruning across convolutional layers for VGG-19 and Resnet-18 to avoid bottlenecking small-parameter layers; this global pruning interacts with learning-rate sensitivity and is part of the hyperparameter considerations that enable finding smaller winning tickets in deep, parameter-heterogeneous networks. This global-vs-layer-wise pruning point is discussed and empirically compared in the appendices. Fig. 38

Conclude that, for the deeper networks examined, the ability of iterative pruning with resetting to discover winning tickets depends sensitively on optimizer hyperparameters—particularly the initial learning rate—but that linear learning-rate warmup from 0 to the original initial rate over an appropriately chosen number of iterations $k$ restores winning-ticket discovery at higher initial rates; the authors present concrete warmup settings (e.g., $k=10000$ for VGG-19 at initial rate 0.1 and $k=20000$ for Resnet-18 at initial rate 0.03) that empirically enable winning-ticket identification under the reported regimes.

Begin from the established existence of winning tickets (Conclusion 1). State that the authors performed targeted empirical analyses of the structural and initialization properties of discovered winning tickets (Appendix F) primarily on the Lenet experiments with both Adam and SGD optimizers, and that these analyses produce several empirical characterizations.

Characterization (a) — distributional change of surviving initial weight values: the authors examine the distributions of initial weights for the connections that survive pruning (i.e., the initial values in $\\theta_0$ for indices where $m=1$). They report that these per-layer distributions become non-Gaussian and often bimodal as pruning proceeds, with layer-dependent asymmetries in sign and magnitude (for example, the second hidden layer and output layer become increasingly bimodal while the input layer may maintain its distribution). These distributional plots and observations are presented in Appendix F (Figures 15 and 16). Fig. 15

Characterization (b) — surviving weights change more during training: to examine whether surviving weights were already near their final values or changed substantially during optimization, the authors compute the magnitude of the difference between initial and final weights in the unpruned network and compare the distributions for weights that survive pruning versus those that do not. They find that surviving (winning-ticket) weights typically undergo larger changes in magnitude between initialization and final trained state than pruned weights, indicating that surviving weights are not merely already close to final values but actually move more during training. This analysis and the supporting histograms are given in Appendix F (Figures 19 and 20). Fig. 19

Characterization (c) — reinitializing from the empirical per-layer winning-ticket distribution and robustness to added Gaussian noise: define $\\mathcal{D}_m$ as the empirical per-layer distribution of winning-ticket initializations (i.e., the set of initial values of surviving connections). The authors sample new per-layer initializations from $\\mathcal{D}_m$ (rather than from the original Gaussian $\\mathcal{D}_\\theta$) and train $f(x;m\\odot\\theta_0')$; they report that this reinitialization from $\\mathcal{D}_m$ does not recover the original winning-ticket performance (Appendix F.3, Figure 17). Separately, the authors add Gaussian noise to the winning-ticket initializations with standard deviations scaled relative to the layer's initialization standard deviation (noise levels $0.5\\sigma$, $\\sigma$, $2\\sigma$, $3\\sigma$) and report that small noise ($0.5\\sigma$) has little effect but larger noise degrades performance gradually; even with moderate noise, these re-noised initializations often still outperform fully random reinitialization. These experiments are described in Appendix F.3 and F.7 and plotted (Figure 25). Fig. 17Fig. 25

Characterization (d) — incoming vs outgoing connectivity post-pruning: the authors analyze node-level connectivity after pruning. They compute the fraction of incoming connections retained per unit and find that incoming connectivity of units tends to be approximately proportional across units (i.e., units retain incoming edges roughly in proportion to the layer's overall sparsity), indicating no extreme imbalance in incoming degree. In contrast, the fraction of outgoing connections retained per unit is often highly uneven: some units retain many more outgoing connections than others, producing multi-modal outgoing-degree distributions, particularly for the input layer in Lenet. These connectivity histograms are shown in Appendix F (Figures 21–24). Fig. 21Fig. 23

Note optimizer-robustness of these phenomena: the authors report that these structural and initialization phenomena are consistent across the optimizers examined (Adam and SGD) for the Lenet and Conv experiments that they analyzed, with differences in the precise shapes but qualitative agreement (e.g., bimodality and outgoing-degree unevenness appear for both optimizers). This cross-optimizer consistency is discussed in Appendix F and illustrated in paired plots for Adam vs. SGD. Fig. 16

Conclude that the experimental characterizations (a) through (d) summarize the empirical structural and initialization properties of winning tickets in the examined settings: (a) surviving initial weights become non-Gaussian and often bimodal, (b) surviving weights tend to change more during training than pruned weights, (c) sampling from the empirical winning-ticket initialization distribution $\\mathcal{D}_m$ or adding moderate Gaussian noise does not fully recover original winning-ticket performance (though small noise is tolerated), and (d) incoming connectivity per unit is roughly proportional while outgoing connectivity can be highly uneven.

Treat the established result that pruning+reset uncovers winning tickets (Conclusion 1) as given. Define the distinction between layer-wise magnitude pruning (prune within each layer at the same per-layer rate) and global magnitude pruning (consider all convolutional-layer weights together and prune the lowest-magnitude weights across those layers collectively).

Explain the motivation the authors provide for global pruning on very deep, parameter-heterogeneous networks: in networks like VGG-19 and Resnet-18, convolutional layers vary dramatically in parameter counts (for VGG-19, earlier layers may have thousands while latter layers have millions), so pruning each layer at the same per-layer rate can over-prune small layers and create bottlenecks that prevent discovering smaller winning tickets; pruning globally avoids imposing identical per-layer removal quotas and thus can preserve capacity in small-parameter layers while reducing parameters in large layers. This conjectured rationale is stated when introducing global pruning in Section 4 and Appendix I.1. Fig. 38

Present the empirical comparison the authors make between global and layer-wise pruning on VGG-19 and Resnet-18: the authors run iterative pruning with both strategies and compare the smallest $P_m$ at which they could still find subnetworks that match or approach original accuracy. For VGG-19 (with their described training regime and warmup settings), global pruning produced winning tickets at $P_m \\approx 1.5\\%$, whereas layer-wise pruning only produced winning tickets down to $P_m \\approx 6.9\\%$ under the same hyperparameters; this large gap is explicitly reported in Appendix I.1 and shown in the comparison plots. Fig. 38

Note the similar but milder effect for Resnet-18: global pruning also finds smaller winning tickets for Resnet-18 than layer-wise pruning in the experiments, though the difference in minimal $P_m$ is less extreme than for VGG-19. The comparative plots and text in Appendix I.1 document this behavior. Fig. 39

Conclude that, for very deep networks whose convolutional layers have highly uneven parameter counts (for example VGG-19, Resnet-18), global magnitude pruning across convolutional layers enables finding smaller winning tickets (smaller $P_m$) than pruning each layer separately at the same per-layer rates, because global pruning avoids bottlenecking small-parameter layers under the experimental regimes the authors tested.

open_questions.content: The paper identifies several unresolved scientific and practical issues left open by the present empirical study: (1) scalability and generality: whether winning tickets exist and can be discovered efficiently for large-scale datasets and models used in practice (notably ImageNet-scale training and production-scale architectures), since iterative pruning as used here is computationally intensive and was evaluated only on MNIST and CIFAR10; (2) search efficiency: how to design more efficient algorithms or heuristics (beyond repeated full training runs) that discover winning tickets with substantially less compute; (3) pruning and architecture formats: whether structured pruning (filters, channels, or other hardware-friendly sparsity) or non-magnitude-based pruning procedures can locate winning tickets that are both smaller and better suited to modern hardware and libraries; (4) initialization mechanism: what precise properties of the original initializations and their joint arrangement with the sparse connectivity confer trainability (the underlying optimization-landscape explanation is unresolved); (5) optimization sensitivity: why discovery of winning tickets in deeper networks depends on learning-rate choices and why warmup mitigates this sensitivity—whether alternative identification schemes can remove the need for warmup; (6) theoretical connections: whether and under what conditions SGD inherently seeks out and trains well-initialized subnetworks (the "lottery ticket conjecture"), i.e., whether the existence of a winning ticket is necessary or sufficient for SGD to reach particular test accuracies; and (7) transferability and design: whether winning tickets (architecture+initialization pairs) discovered on one task or dataset can be transferred to other tasks, and whether winning-ticket structure can systematically inspire improved architecture and initialization design. These issues are explicitly framed in the paper as limitations and directions for future work and remain unresolved by the experiments presented.
